Celsius reached '$1 billion brand status at retail' on a trailing-52-week basis as of April 26, 2023; category share roughly doubled from 3.7% to 8% over twelve months.
The October 2022 transition from independent Anheuser-Busch distributors to PepsiCo drove ACV to 95% far faster than the 12-18 months internally expected.
~68% of Celsius sales are incremental to the category (24% new-to-category plus 44% user intensification) - retailers value this as not just brand shifting.
Management is 'hyper paranoid' about competition - Celsius is the uncomfortable #3 brand with players above and below; defense is focus, execution and constant reinvention.
1H 2023 gross margin pressure stems from destabilizing the low-mileage 'orbit' shipping model during the Pepsi integration; management declined to quantify the pressure.
Management reaffirmed mid-40s gross margin for 2023, with upper-mid-40s achievable in 2H and over the next two-to-three years via vertical integration.
A structural comparability nuance vs Monster: Celsius includes outbound freight in COGS whereas Monster classifies it as a selling expense - the headline Monster margin overstates the gap.
2024 is positioned as a 'superior' year - the first fully integrated into Pepsi's annual operating plan (AOP); Celsius integrated October 1, 2022 outside the 2023 AOP.
Pricing posture is cautious amid macro uncertainty - Celsius took ~6% pricing in 2022 but the full benefit will not flow through given promotional deal-downs.
Retailers are requesting more promotions because they are 'hearing some traffic slowing down' - a softer demand signal; ~24 promotional weeks/year is the category norm.
The club channel (Costco, Sam's, BJ's) carries higher cost from reworking/repacking; the move from a hand-packed 15-pack to an in-line 18-pack improved efficiency.
Energy is gaining shelf space as teas, juices and waters get consolidated; lead players try to fragment the energy door, but Celsius's key-accounts team won bull's-eye placements.
International expansion (UK, Canada, Germany, Japan, Australia - existing energy markets) could begin late Q4 2023 into Q1 2024, methodical and tactical, leveraging Pepsi bottlers.
Amazon is key to the omnichannel strategy - Celsius holds 19% on Amazon as the #2 brand, a few points from #1, even as retail ACV expanded.
Spring reset visibility will be clear by late June 2023; SKUs per location rose to 13.6 from ~8, with most growth in convenience (3-4 SKUs a year ago, nearing double digits).
What have been the key drivers behind the doubling of share, and how much did the Pepsi relationship boost performance?

John Fieldly: Celsius continued bringing new consumers into the category, growing ACV and building retailer relationships; the October Pepsi partnership shifted distribution from independent Anheuser-Busch distributors to a national Pepsi network and helped reach 95% ACV at quarter-end - far faster than the internally expected 12-18 months.
Where is Celsius sourcing share from, given it appears to be bringing incremental consumers into the category?

Toby David: ~24% of consumers are new to the category and another 44% are user intensification, totaling ~68% incremental; share sourced is predominantly Red Bull and Monster (70%+ of category) plus capitalizing on Bang's disruption. John Fieldly: Celsius's 'new age energy' positioning makes it truly incremental, with 10% of Pepsi sales now in the untracked food-service channel.
Is a 10% share within reach given the momentum, and is another doubling possible by next year?

John Fieldly: yes - Celsius reported 7.5 share at March 26, reached 8 share by April 26 (a 0.5-point gain in 30 days) vs 3.7 a year earlier, with velocity increasing despite added distribution. Toby David cited ~22% share in South Florida and 19% on Amazon as runway evidence; Fieldly cited new markets like Buffalo and flagged the no-sugar push as a further opportunity.
Celsius achieved its gains despite stepped-up competition - how worried is management and how does it defend its share?

John Fieldly: Celsius is 'hyper paranoid'; competition is fierce in a double-digit-growth category and Celsius is the #3 brand - an uncomfortable position with players above and below; the defense is focus, execution against annual operating plans, constant reinvention, and connecting with new consumer segments (e.g., MMA partnerships).
How does the innovation pipeline compare to last year, and are 2024 plans flavor or package innovation?

John Fieldly: cited the green apple cherry SKU (a 7-Eleven partnership, one of their fastest-growing SKUs) and a lemon lime flavor launched with Walmart. For 2024, focus stays on the core portfolio with fruit-forward innovation plus further innovation on the 16-oz Celsius HEAT line; timing and sequencing are the main consideration given the recent 95% ACV achievement.
How much incremental shelf or cooler space did Celsius gain during the spring resets, and has it been quantified?

Toby David: as of March 26 Celsius was at 13.6 SKUs per location (MULO+C), up from ~8 a year prior, with most growth from convenience (3-4 SKUs a year ago, nearing double digits now); full reset visibility comes by late June. The Bang disruption and an aggressive sales organization helped, and the incrementality story resonates with retailers.
Where shelf space is sourced from
Where are retailers sourcing the incremental energy shelf space from, and are they allocating dedicated better-for-you energy space?

John Fieldly: incremental energy space appears to come from consolidating teas, juices and waters; lead players try to fragment the energy door to protect bull's-eye placement, pushing newer brands into 'the gutter,' but Celsius positions as total energy and its key-accounts team moved it into bull's-eye placements.
How much pricing did Celsius implement over the last 12-18 months, when, and are there plans for incremental pricing this year?

John Fieldly: Celsius took an average ~6% price increase last year; while there is room for more, macro conditions make management cautious and it may prefer supply-chain leverage over frontline pricing; a pricing committee meets monthly, and promotions are increasing so the full 6% will not flow through.
Does Celsius plan to step up promotions in line with what competitors are doing over the summer?

John Fieldly: retailers are asking for more promotion because they see traffic slowing; promotions are key for the summer '100 days of summer' season and off-shelf placements. Roughly 24 weeks a year are promotional in energy, and management does not expect promotions to materially impact gross margin.
Can management quantify the first-half gross margin pressure from integrating the new distribution system, and are back-half efficiencies expected?

Toby David: the Pepsi transition went smoothly; Celsius took a conservative 1H approach because of its 'orbit' model - destabilized in Q1 and partly Q2 to keep product on shelf (e.g., shipping from the Pacific Northwest to Dallas). Celsius still anticipates mid-40s gross margin in 1H with possible upside and upper-mid-40s in 2H; no specific number provided.
Is Celsius operating back within its orbits now, or will that take more months?

Toby David: each month is improving with fewer out-of-orbit shipments, but full synchronization with Pepsi takes the full year; Pepsi plans ~three years ahead and Celsius integrated October 1 outside the 2023 AOP, making 2024 the first cohesive year. John Fieldly: vertical-integration roadmaps over the next two-to-three years should drive further margin.
Is there a realistic gross margin target over the next several years beyond the mid-40s for 2023?

John Fieldly: reiterated mid-40s for 2023 with upper-mid-40s achievable via vertical integration; flagged that Celsius includes outbound freight in COGS while Monster treats it as a selling expense - relevant when benchmarking.
Will sales and marketing expense increase or step up to remain competitive and drive awareness?

John Fieldly: household penetration remains low with opportunity; S&M runs ~22-23% of sales (lower in Q1, higher in Q4 on event timing); leverage to be gained as the company grows, but Celsius must invest ahead of brand growth given ACV just hit 95%; cited Q2/Q3 summer programs (Oasis Vibe launch, central vibe store, Target partnership).
Innovation requires constant reinvention to stay relevant and continue innovating with flavors.
John Fieldly agreed briefly - 'You do. You got to continue to reinvent yourself.'
How important is the e-commerce channel to future growth, given Celsius's 19% Amazon share as the second-largest energy brand there?

John Fieldly: Amazon has been key to the omnichannel strategy from the start; holding 19% as the #2 brand (a few points from #1) even as retail ACV expanded is notable; Celsius is also doing well in the club channel entered ~12 months prior.
What is the margin impact or headwind of the club channel?

John Fieldly: the club channel requires additional reworking and repacking, adding cost, but management remains confident in mid-40s margin by year-end; margin is a function of mix, and moving from a hand-packed 15-pack to an in-line 18-pack improved efficiency and capacity.
Can you give more color on the international expansion plans (said to begin early next year), how big an investment, and Pepsi's role?

Toby David: Celsius works closely with Pepsi (its preferred international distributor, mostly using third-party bottlers) to ensure pricing works for all margins; after the US, priority markets are the UK, Canada, Germany, Japan and Australia - existing energy markets; entry could come late Q4 2023 into Q1 2024, a small percentage of revenue (consensus over $1B for 2023), methodical and tactical. John Fieldly stressed entering markets successfully, not 'spray and pray.'
